drills.name: Ma bu
drills.desc: The foundation stance of Chinese martial arts: feet wide, thighs sinking toward parallel, spine vertical, fists chambered at the hips. Traditional schools measure progress in minutes held — the stance forges leg endurance, breath control, and the rooted structure every technique launches from. Sink lower as the legs strengthen; never let the posture buy comfort.
mistakes: Knees collapsing inward instead of tracking over the toes.
Hips tilting forward and arching the lower back.
Rising taller as fatigue builds instead of holding the set depth.

drills.name: Gong bu
drills.desc: The long forward stance: front knee bent over the toes, rear leg straight and driving, hips square to the front. It is the delivery platform for straight punches and palm strikes — power flows from the rear foot's push through the squared hips. Transitioning cleanly between ma bu and gong bu is the first footwork skill.
mistakes: Rear heel lifting off the floor, breaking the drive line.
Hips left angled sideways instead of squared to the front.
Front knee sliding past the toes under load.

drills.name: Five-stance transitions
drills.alt: Flowing between ma bu, gong bu, xu bu, pu bu, xie bu
drills.desc: Linking the five basic stances in a continuous flow while the head stays level and the hips stay low. The skill is transferring weight smoothly through the low positions without bobbing up to rest — the legs work like pistons under a still torso. This drill is the mobility-under-load engine of all forms work.
mistakes: Standing up between stances instead of staying low through the transition.
Rushing the flow and arriving in shallow, unset positions.
Eyes dropping to the feet instead of staying on an imagined opponent.

drills.name: Chong quan
drills.desc: The basic corkscrew punch fired from the hip chamber, usually drilled in ma bu or gong bu in alternating chains. The fist rotates palm-down at full extension while the opposite hand snaps back to the hip with equal force. Drilled in long sets, it welds hip, waist, and shoulder into one delivery system.
mistakes: Punching from the shoulder while the waist stays frozen.
Weak pulling hand — the returning fist powers the outgoing one.
Wrist bending at extension instead of a straight line to the first two knuckles.

drills.name: Lian huan quan
drills.desc: Rapid alternating straight punches down the center line, each fist rolling over the last in an unbroken chain. Speed comes from relaxation — the arms stay loose between impacts while the elbows track close to the ribs. The drill trains the center-line dominance that styles like Wing Chun are built around.
mistakes: Elbows flaring wide off the center line between punches.
Tensing the shoulders, which throttles the chain's speed.
Reaching forward with the torso instead of keeping structure and letting the fists cycle.

drills.name: Tui zhang
drills.desc: An open-palm thrust that drives the heel of the hand through the target with the whole body behind it. The wrist cocks back late so the palm arrives structurally stacked over the forearm, transferring leg drive without risking the knuckles. It teaches issuing force from the ground up — fa jin in its simplest form.

exercises.name: Medicine ball push throws from split stance

mistakes: Striking with the fingers or flat palm instead of the heel of the hand.
Pushing with the arm after the body has stopped moving.
Locking the elbow violently at full extension.

drills.name: Deng tui
drills.desc: A straight kick that chambers the knee and drives the heel forward with the toes pulled back. Unlike a snapping toe kick it thrusts through the target, borrowing the hip's forward drive. It doubles as a stop-kick against an advancing opponent and as the base pattern for all thrusting kicks.
mistakes: Kicking with pointed toes instead of leading with the heel.
Leaning far back and losing the hip drive forward.
No re-chamber — the leg drops straight down after impact.

drills.name: Tan tui
drills.desc: A low, whipping snap kick to shin or knee height, flicked out from the knee like a released spring and paired with hand techniques above it. The famous Tan Tui line routines chain it with punches so the hands and feet learn to arrive together. Its virtues are speed, disguise, and never compromising the stance.
mistakes: Lifting the whole leg from the hip instead of snapping from the knee.
Kicking high and slow when the technique lives low and fast.
Hands going dead while the leg works — tan tui is a hands-and-feet rhythm.

drills.name: Ce chuai tui
drills.desc: The kung fu side kick: knee chambered across the body, hips stacked, then the heel driven out on a straight line with the torso counterbalancing. Wushu practice adds a held extension — pausing the kick mid-air — which builds the hip strength that makes the fast version effortless. Control equals power here.
mistakes: Hips unstacked so the kick pushes diagonally instead of piercing.
Dropping the torso to the floor to fake height.
Striking with the flat foot instead of heel and blade.

drills.name: Bai lian jiao
drills.desc: A straight-leg kick swept up the center line and out in a wide arc, slapping the outside edge of the foot into the raised palm in training. It opens the hip in the opposite direction from most kicks, building the rotational range that spinning techniques depend on. Height and sweep grow from hamstring and hip mobility, not brute swing.
mistakes: Bending the knee mid-arc, collapsing the sweep.
Rotating the whole torso with the kick instead of keeping the chest square.
Swinging from momentum only, with no control at the top of the arc.

drills.name: Xuan feng jiao
drills.desc: The wushu tornado kick: a running or stepping 360-degree jump spin finishing with an inside crescent kick that slaps the opposite palm mid-air. The cross-step converts sprint momentum into rotation, the arms wrap hard to accelerate the spin, and the kick fires at the top of the jump. It is the gateway technique to all aerial kicks.
mistakes: Jumping before the cross-step finishes, so the spin has no stored rotation.
Arms hanging loose instead of wrapping to whip the turn.
Kicking on the way down instead of at the peak of the jump.

drills.name: Hu zhua
drills.desc: The tiger shape: fingers clawed and tensed, striking with the palm heel then raking or seizing on the recoil. Tiger work is direct and heavy — deep stances, aggressive forward pressure, and crushing grip strength turned into strikes. Conditioning the hands and forearms is half the style.
mistakes: Claw shape held rigid the whole time instead of tensing only at contact.
Slapping with the fingers rather than driving the palm heel first.
All arm, no stance — tiger power is bodyweight moving forward.

drills.name: Tang lang gou
drills.desc: The mantis hook: wrist flexed into a hook that snags the opponent's arm, redirects it, and clears the line for an instant counter. Techniques chain in rapid grab-strike rhythms, demanding fast, precise wrists and elastic shoulders. It trains the trapping-hand sensitivity that separates mantis boxing from pure striking styles.
mistakes: Grabbing and holding on instead of hooking, redirecting, and striking in one beat.
Wrist too soft, letting the hook collapse under the opponent's arm.
Watching the trapping hand instead of the opponent's center.

drills.name: Wu bu quan
drills.desc: The first form of modern wushu: a short routine linking the five fundamental stances with basic punches, blocks, and a snap kick. It is judged on depth of stance, clean shapes, and a level head throughout the transitions. Every long form is built from the vocabulary this routine installs.
mistakes: Shallow stances that make the form easier but empty.
Head bobbing up and down through the transitions.
Performing shapes without intent — every movement should strike or defend something.

drills.name: Zheng ti tui
drills.desc: A straight-leg swing kick toward the forehead, walked in lines with the torso upright and the standing leg locked. It is flexibility training disguised as kicking: each rep actively stretches the hamstring at speed, building the loose, controlled hips wushu kicking demands. Height is earned rep by rep, never yanked.
mistakes: Leaning the torso back to buy height instead of keeping it tall.
Bending either knee — both legs stay straight throughout.
Kicking with momentum only and slamming the leg down uncontrolled.

drills.name: Ya tui
drills.desc: The classical leg-pressing routine: heel on a bar or rail at waist height and above, folding the chest to the shin in front, side, and back positions. Done daily it is the engine behind wushu's high kicks and full splits. The press is patient and breathing-led — force applied gradually on the exhale, never bounced.
mistakes: Bouncing into the stretch instead of pressing gradually with the breath.
Rounding the spine to reach the shin rather than folding from the hips.
Only stretching the favorite leg and building a lopsided kicking range.
